subject: Physics
description: Concave/convex mirrors, focal length, real vs virtual, image formation, mirror formula

questions.stem: When light is reflected off a smooth (specular) surface, the laws of reflection state that:

options.option_text: Angle of incidence > angle of reflection
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from normal); incident ray, reflected ray, normal lie in one plane
Reflected ray bends towards the surface
Light always travels through the mirror

questions.explanation: Two laws of reflection: (1) angle of incidence (i) = angle of reflection (r) — both from the NORMAL to the surface, not from the surface itself. (2) the incident ray, reflected ray and normal at the point of incidence are co-planar. Hold for both regular (specular, polished) and diffuse (rough) reflection at every point — but rough surfaces have varied normals, so reflected rays scatter.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A CONCAVE mirror, when an object is placed BEYOND its centre of curvature C, forms an image that is:

options.option_text: Real, inverted, diminished — between F and C

questions.explanation: Concave (converging) mirror image table: object at infinity → image at F (point); beyond C → between F and C (real, inverted, diminished — used in telescope mirrors); at C → at C (real, inverted, same size); between C and F → beyond C (real, inverted, magnified — projector); at F → at infinity (highly magnified); between P and F → behind mirror (virtual, erect, magnified — shaving / makeup mirror).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A CONVEX mirror always forms an image that is:

options.option_text: Virtual, erect, diminished — irrespective of object position

questions.explanation: Convex (diverging) mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image, located between P (pole) and F (behind mirror). That's why convex mirrors are used as REAR-VIEW MIRRORS — wider field of view, all images upright. Side-view mirrors carry warning 'Objects in mirror are closer than they appear' because of the 'diminished' effect. Other uses: security mirrors at shop corners, ATM cabin mirrors, blind-spot mirrors.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The relation between focal length (f) and radius of curvature (R) of a spherical mirror is:
questions.explanation: For a spherical mirror, focal length is half the radius of curvature: f = R/2. Both f and R are measured from the pole P. Sign convention (Cartesian): distances measured from P; positive direction = direction of incident light. Concave: f and R negative; Convex: f and R positive (in the most common convention). Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = −v/u = h_image / h_object.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: An object 4 cm tall is placed 30 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Image distance v is:
questions.explanation: Cartesian sign convention: u = −30 cm (object on left of mirror), f = −20 cm (concave). Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f → 1/v − 1/30 = −1/20 → 1/v = −1/20 + 1/30 = (−3 + 2)/60 = −1/60 → v = −60 cm. Negative → real image on same side as object. Magnification m = −v/u = −(−60)/(−30) = −2 → image is inverted (negative sign), 2× size = 8 cm tall. Positioned 60 cm from mirror.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A 'real image' formed by a mirror or lens is one that:

options.option_text: Cannot be obtained on a screen
Can be obtained on a screen — light rays actually meet at the image point

questions.explanation: Real image — light rays actually converge → projectable onto a screen. Always inverted (top-bottom flipped). Formed by concave mirrors/converging lenses when object is beyond the focal point. Examples: cinema projector, camera, eye, microscope, refracting telescope. Virtual image — rays only APPEAR to come from a point (extending divergent rays backwards) → not projectable. Formed by plane mirrors, convex mirrors, diverging lenses, and concave mirrors with object inside f.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The image formed in a plane mirror is:

options.option_text: Virtual, erect, same size; laterally inverted; image distance behind = object distance in front

questions.explanation: Plane mirror — virtual, erect, same size as object. Image distance behind mirror = object distance in front. Laterally inverted (left↔right swap; top-bottom NOT swapped — that's why text appears mirror-flipped). Used in periscope (combination of two), kaleidoscope, optical instruments. Plane mirror is essentially a spherical mirror with R = ∞, so f = ∞ → image at the mirror level (using mirror formula 1/v = 1/f − 1/u gives v = −u).
